formulations.label: Tablets
formulations.note: No UK SmPC was found for a 1000 mg tablet; the UK 500 mg tablet SmPC is used. A 1000 mg tablet equals the stated maximum daily dose for adults and children over 12 years.

src.q: Each tablet contains 500mg of Ascorbic Acid
Maximum daily doses: Adults and children over 12 years, 1000 mg.

bnf.note: BNF/BNFC is only available in the UK; not accessed.

items.t: Treatment of vitamin C deficiency, including treatment and prevention of scurvy.

src.q: For the treatment of Vitamin C deficiency including the treatment and prevention of scurvy.

restrictions.note: No prescribing restrictions in the UK ascorbic acid 500 mg tablet SmPC.

items.t: Adults and elderly: not less than 250 mg daily in divided doses; maximum 1000 mg a day.

src.q: Treatment: Not less than 250 mg daily in divided doses.
Maximum daily doses: Adults and children over 12 years, 1000 mg.

items.t: Children over 4 years: not less than 250 mg daily in divided doses. Maximum: 500 mg a day at 4-11 years; 1000 mg a day over 12 years. No dose given under 4 years.

src.q: Adults and children over 4 years: Treatment: Not less than 250 mg daily in divided doses.
Children 4 - 11 years, 500 mg.

items.t: Hypersensitivity to ascorbic acid or any excipient.

src.q: Hypersensitivity to ascorbic acid or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1.

items.t: Hyperoxaluria.

src.q: Ascorbic acid should not be given to patients with hyperoxaluria.

items.t: Long-term high intake raises renal clearance of vitamin C; stopping suddenly may cause deficiency.

src.q: Increased intake of ascorbic acid over a prolonged period may result in an increased renal clearance of ascorbic acid, and deficiency may result if the intake is reduced or withdrawn rapidly

items.t: G6PD deficiency: ascorbic acid has been implicated in haemolytic anaemia.

src.q: Ascorbic acid has been implicated in precipitating haemolytic anaemia in certain individuals with a deficiency of glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase.

items.t: Interferes with laboratory tests: urine and blood glucose, uric acid, creatinine; high doses can give false-negative faecal occult blood tests.

src.q: Ascorbic acid may interfere with tests and assays for urinary glucose
High doses of ascorbic acid may give false negative readings in faecal occult blood tests.

items.t: Contains lactose: not for people with hereditary fructose or galactose intolerance, total lactase deficiency, glucose-galactose malabsorption or sucrase-isomaltase insufficiency.

src.q: Patients with rare hereditary problems of fructose or galactose intolerance, total lactase deficiency, glucose-galactose malabsorption or sucrase-isomaltase insufficiency should not take this medicine as it contains lactose.

items.t: Taking antacids with ascorbic acid is not recommended, especially in renal insufficiency. Aluminium-containing antacids: urinary aluminium elimination may increase.

src.q: Concurrent administration of antacids and ascorbic acid is not recommended, especially in patients with renal insufficiency.
Concomitant administration of aluminium-containing antacids may increase urinary aluminium elimination.

items.t: Ascorbic acid may increase oral iron absorption.

src.q: Ascorbic acid may increase the oral absorption of iron.

items.t: With desferrioxamine: increased urinary iron excretion and risk of cardiovascular adverse effects; use with caution and monitor cardiac function.

src.q: Ascorbic acid should be used with caution in patients receiving desferrioxamine and cardiac function should be monitored.

items.t: Aspirin may reduce ascorbic acid absorption; aspirin's effect is not reduced.

src.q: Concomitant administration of aspirin and ascorbic acid may interfere with absorption of ascorbic acid.
Renal excretion of salicylate is not affected and does not lead to reduced anti-inflammatory effects of aspirin.

items.t: May reduce amphetamine absorption. With amygdalin (a complementary medicine) can cause cyanide toxicity.

src.q: Ascorbic acid may reduce the absorption of amphetamines.
Co-administration with amygdalin (a complementary medicine) can cause cyanide toxicity.

items.t: No renal dose advice given. Avoid antacids with ascorbic acid, especially in renal insufficiency. Massive overdose can cause renal failure; large doses can cause renal oxalate stones.

src.q: Concurrent administration of antacids and ascorbic acid is not recommended, especially in patients with renal insufficiency.
Large doses of ascorbic acid may cause diarrhoea and the formation of renal oxalate calculi.
Renal failure can occur with massive ascorbic acid overdosage.

hepatic.note: No hepatic impairment advice in the UK ascorbic acid 500 mg tablet SmPC.

items.t: No clinical data in pregnancy; animal studies show no harm. Pregnant women should exercise caution.

src.q: For ascorbic acid no clinical data on exposed pregnancies are available.
Pregnant women should exercise caution.

items.t: Excreted in breast milk; caution, but no evidence of harm to the infant.

src.q: Ascorbic acid is excreted in breast milk. Though again caution should be exercised, no evidence exists suggesting such excretion is hazardous to the infant.

items.t: No fertility data.

src.q: Fertility No data available.

items.t: Large doses may cause diarrhoea; doses over 600 mg have a diuretic effect.

src.q: Large doses of ascorbic acid may cause diarrhoea.
Doses of more than 600mg have a diuretic effect.

items.t: Haemolytic anaemia in some people with G6PD deficiency.

src.q: Ascorbic acid has been implicated in precipitating haemolytic anaemia in certain individuals with a deficiency of glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase.

items.t: People at risk of hyperoxaluria should not take more than 1 gram a day (increased urinary oxalate).

src.q: Patients known to be at risk of hyperoxaluria should not ingest ascorbic acid in doses exceeding 1 gram daily, as there may be increased urinary oxalate excretion.

monitoring.note: No routine monitoring stated in the UK ascorbic acid 500 mg tablet SmPC (only cardiac monitoring with desferrioxamine; see interactions).

items.t: Oral; give the daily dose in divided doses.

src.q: Treatment: Not less than 250 mg daily in divided doses.

items.t: Do not take more than the maximum daily dose; large doses can cause diarrhoea and kidney stones.

src.q: Large doses of ascorbic acid may cause diarrhoea and the formation of renal oxalate calculi.

items.t: Tell the laboratory you take vitamin C: it can affect blood and urine sugar tests and stool blood tests.

src.q: Ascorbic acid may interfere with biochemical determinations of creatinine, uric acid and glucose in samples of blood and urine.
Hypersensitivity to ascorbic acid or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1.

rules.consequence: Increased urinary oxalate; oxalate kidney stones.
rules.action: Do not give (SmPC 4.3). Patients at risk of hyperoxaluria: not more than 1 gram daily.
rules.sourceWording: should not be given to patients with hyperoxaluria

src.q: Ascorbic acid should not be given to patients with hyperoxaluria.
Patients known to be at risk of hyperoxaluria should not ingest ascorbic acid in doses exceeding 1 gram daily, as there may be increased urinary oxalate excretion.

rules.action: Be aware of the risk of haemolysis (no specific action stated).
rules.sourceWording: has been implicated in precipitating haemolytic anaemia

src.q: Ascorbic acid has been implicated in precipitating haemolytic anaemia in certain individuals with a deficiency of glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase.
Ascorbic acid may cause acidosis or haemolytic anaemia in certain individuals with a deficiency of glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase.
